name: Melrose Abbey
summary: The Cistercian abbey founded in the Scottish Borders by David I in 1136, wrecked repeatedly in the Anglo-Scottish wars, and the burial place of the heart of Robert the Bruce.
overview: Melrose Abbey was the first Cistercian house in Scotland, founded by David I in 1136 with monks from Rievaulx in Yorkshire.
Its position in the Borders made it rich in wool and repeatedly ruinous in war, and a lead casket found beneath its chapter house is taken to hold the heart of Robert the Bruce.

imageInfo.caption: The ruined abbey church at Melrose in the Scottish Borders, mostly rebuilding of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, in a 2004 photograph.
imageInfo.creator: Globaltraveller (Wikimedia Commons)
imageInfo.note: Almost nothing visible belongs to the abbey David I founded in 1136. The church was rebuilt after Edward II's army wrecked it in 1322 and again after Richard II burned it in 1385, so the elaborate tracery and carving shown here is late medieval work, left roofless after the English invasion of 1544.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Melrose Abbey stands on the south bank of the Tweed in the Scottish Borders. David I founded it in 1136 as the first Cistercian house in Scotland, settling it with monks sent from Rievaulx in North Yorkshire, itself a daughter of Cîteaux, and the abbey church was dedicated on 28 July 1146.

The house became one of the wealthiest religious corporations in the kingdom, and one of the most exposed. Everything that made its site attractive — good land, the Tweed, the road south — also placed it directly on the route every English army took into Scotland.

contentSections.title: Old Melrose and the new site
paragraphs: There was a monastery in the area five centuries before the Cistercians arrived. Old Melrose, about two miles east inside a loop of the Tweed, was founded from Lindisfarne in the seventh century under Aidan, and Cuthbert entered it as a young man and served as its prior before moving to Lindisfarne about 664.

The Cistercians did not reuse that site. David I's monks settled two miles west at the place now called Melrose, leaving the older foundation as a chapel and a memory, which is why the abbey ruins and the Cuthbert associations belong to two different places with nearly the same name.

contentSections.title: Wool and land
paragraphs: Cistercian houses were built to farm, and Melrose farmed at scale. Its granges spread across Lauderdale, Teviotdale and the Lammermuir hills, worked by lay brothers, and the abbey ran very large flocks whose wool was sold to Flemish and Italian merchants.

That trade tied a Border monastery into the commercial networks of the Low Countries and made its income worth fighting over. The abbey also held fishings on the Tweed, salt pans, and burgh property, and its cartulary is one of the fullest records of how a Scottish religious house actually made its money.

contentSections.title: The border wars
paragraphs: The abbey was damaged in the Wars of Scottish Independence and never afterwards left alone for long. In 1322 Edward II's army wrecked the buildings; Robert the Bruce paid for the rebuilding and the work was audited by Sir James Douglas, and the king left money to the house in his will.

In 1385 the army of Richard II burned it again, and the reconstruction that followed produced the elaborate late Gothic church whose ruins stand today, with its famous carved detail including the bagpipe-playing pig on a roof spout. The English invasion of 1544, during the war known as the Rough Wooing, inflicted damage that was never repaired.

contentSections.title: The heart of Robert the Bruce
paragraphs: Robert the Bruce died in June 1329 having vowed to take his crusading debt to the Holy Land, and asked that his heart be carried there. Sir James Douglas set out with it and got as far as Andalusia, where he was killed fighting the Moors at Teba in 1330. The heart was brought back and buried at Melrose, by tradition in 1331.

A lead casket was found beneath the chapter house in a 1921 excavation, reburied, and located again in 1996. It was opened, examined, and reburied at the abbey on 22 June 1998 under a memorial stone. No DNA testing was carried out, so the identification rests on the place, the container and the tradition rather than on physical proof, which is the honest limit of what is known.

contentSections.title: The end of the abbey
paragraphs: Monastic life at Melrose dwindled through the sixteenth century rather than ending at a stroke. The community was not dispersed by a single act of suppression; the last monk died in 1590, and the house was formally disestablished in 1609, its lands passing into secular hands.

Part of the nave was walled off and used as a parish church into the eighteenth century. The ruins were taken into state care in the nineteenth century, and Alexander II of Scotland, who died in 1249, lies buried within them alongside a number of Douglas lords.
